power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Elevated blood pressure variability (BPV) is predictive of Alzheimer's disease neuropathologic change observed with AD biomarkers.
However, prior studies have largely focused on visit-to-visit BPV, which may be influenced by antihypertensive medication adherence and other external factors.
Few studies have investigated beat-to-beat BPV, a reliable and direct measure of cardiovascular and autonomic function relevant to AD.
Methods: Independently living older adults (N=132) were recruited from the community.
Participants underwent continuous blood pressure monitoring and venipuncture.
Plasma p-Tau 217 , p-Tau 181 , GFAP, NfL, and amyloid-β 42/40 ratio were assessed.

Linear regression examined the relationship between beat-to-beat systolic BPV and plasma AD biomarkers with and without adjustment for age, sex, systolic blood pressure, and apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) carrier status.
Results: Elevated beat-to-beat BPV was associated with elevated plasma p-Tau 217 (β=0.32, p=0.008), plasma p-Tau 181 (β=0.22, p=0.05), and plasma GFAP (β=0.41, p=0.00001).
Elevated BPV was not associated with plasma amyloid-β 42/40 ratio or plasma NfL.

Discussion: Increased beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased Core 1 T 1 biomarkers of phosphorylated and secreted AD tau in blood plasma (i.e., pTau 217 , pTau 181 ), but not with amyloid-β 42/40 ratio, a biomarker more exclusively indexing cerebral amyloid retention alone.
Elevated BPV was also associated with higher plasma GFAP, a marker of astrocyte reactivity.
These findings are consistent with prior studies relating visit-to-visit BPV to AD biomarkers, suggesting that intrinsic cardiovascular and/or autonomic factors underlie links between BPV and AD.

Blood pressure variability (BPV) over various time scales is associated with cerebrovascular disease [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] , neurodegenerative disease 8, 9 , cognitive decline [10] [11] [12] , and dementia 13- 19 .

text.text: Visit-to-visit BPV is a widely used convenience measure of BPV that is associated with accelerated Alzheimer's disease (AD) neuropathologic change reflected in AD biofluid markers and molecular imaging 15, [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] .

text.text: However, questions remain regarding the pathogenesis of visit-tovisit BPV, its test-retest reliability, and the specific mechanisms linking high visit-to-visit BPV to AD pathophysiology.

Blood pressure may vary over months and years between clinic visits due to numerous extraneous factors, including antihypertensive medication adherence and timing, seasonal and diurnal oscillations, temperature, diet and meal timing, psychological stress, and other factors 24 .
text.formatted: Blood pressure may vary over months and years between clinic visits due to numerous extraneous factors, including antihypertensive medication adherence and timing, seasonal and diurnal oscillations, temperature, diet and meal timing, psychological stress, and other factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">24</ref> .

text.text: Thus, it remains unclear whether the relationship between visit-to-visit BPV and AD biomarkers is the product of intrinsic cardiovascular and autonomic factors relevant to AD pathophysiology versus the many extraneous sources of BPV across visits.

Alternatively, beat-to-beat BPV is a valid 25, 26 , high temporal resolution marker of cardiovascular and autonomic function and arterial stiffness 27 that can be acquired reliably 28 in a single clinic visit.

text.text: Only a few small studies have investigated the relationship between beat-tobeat BPV and AD biomarker levels 10, 29 , and these studies have not included plasma p-Tau 217 , a more sensitive and specific marker of amyloid and AD-tau pathophysiology [30] [31] [32] .

text.text: Prior studies suggest that BPV, particularly fluctuations in systolic blood pressure between consecutive cardiac cycles, is more closely associated with AD-tau than with amyloid-β 10, 20 .

text.text: Therefore, the present study will test the a priori hypotheses that higher systolic beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased plasma p-Tau 217 and increased plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), two of the earliest biomarkers of preclinical AD pathophysiology [33] [34] [35] [36] [37] [38] [39] , in order to address current knowledge gaps regarding intrinsic cardiovascular function and its effects on AD pathophysiology.

text.text: Participants were recruited from Los Angeles County and Orange County communities through outreach events, mailing lists, word-of-mouth, online portals, a research volunteer registry, and through the local Alzheimer's Disease Research Center (ADRC).
All procedures were conducted as part of the Vascular Senescence and Cognition (VaSC) Study at the University of Southern California (USC) and the University of California Irvine (UCI).
Older adults aged 60 to 89 years who were living independently were included (Table 1).
text.formatted: Older adults aged 60 to 89 years who were living independently were included (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Study exclusions were a prior diagnosis of dementia, history of clinical stroke, family history of dominantly inherited neurodegenerative disorders, current neurological or major psychiatric disorders that may impact cognitive function, history of moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, active substance abuse, current use of medications impairing the central nervous system, current organ failure or other uncontrolled systemic illness, and contraindications for brain MRI.
Eligibility for the study was verified by a structured clinical health interview and review of current medications with the participant and, when available, a knowledgeable informant study partner.
This study was approved by the USC and UCI Institutional Review Board, and all participants gave informed consent.
The anonymized data that support the findings of this study are available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author, DAN, through appropriate data sharing protocols.
Participants were asked to take medications as normally prescribed and abstain from caffeine on the morning of data collection.
Beat-to-beat blood pressure measurements were obtained continuously during supine rest in a 3 T Siemens MRI scanner, using an MRIcompatible non-invasive continuous BP finger cuff device (Biopac®).
First, the participant rests for 3 min in the supine position prior to the calibration period.

During calibration, BP waveforms are acquired by the continuous monitoring device and two static pressures are simultaneously acquired using a calibrated, MRI-compatible automatic BP device with an inflatable brachial artery cuff (TeslaDUO).
These static pressures are used to calibrate the continuous BP monitor using the Caretaker® system (Biopac®).
After calibration, continuous BP was monitored during MRI for 7 min and further data processing was performed as previously described 28.

text.text: Beat-to-beat BPV is quantified as systolic blood pressure (SBP) average real variability (ARV), a measure of systolic beat-to-beat BPV which has been demonstrated as reliable in older adults 28, 40 regardless of antihypertensive medication use 28 .

One hundred and thirty-six participants underwent continuous BP monitoring and plasma AD biomarker assay.

Two outliers with abnormally high BPV (+3.44 and +7.96 SD), and two outliers with abnormally high p-Tau 217 (+3.21 and +4.34 SD) were removed resulting in a total analyzed sample size of 132 participants.
One participant was also missing plasma GFAP.

text.text: The present study finds that elevated beat-to-beat BPV is associated with increased plasma p-Tau 217 and plasma GFAP, independent of age, sex, systolic blood pressure, APOE4 carrier status, and plasma amyloid-β 42/40 ratio.

Importantly, this is the first study to investigate the relationship between valid 25, 26, 46 and reliable 28 beat-to-beat BPV and plasma p-Tau 217 , a highly sensitive and specific diagnostic and prognostic marker of AD pathophysiology [30] [31] [32].

text.text: Elevated beat-to-beat BPV was not associated with amyloid-β 42/40 and remained associated with p-Tau 217 even after adjustment for amyloid-β 42/40 ratio, confirming previous suggestions 20 that BPV is differentially related to AD-tau (Core 1 T 1 biomarkers 31 ) compared to amyloid pathophysiology (Core 1 A 1 biomarkers 31 ).

text.text: This is consistent with prior findings that arterial stiffness and other vascular risk factors are associated with AD-tau but not amyloid [47] [48] [49] [50].

text.text: Pulse pressure for example was previously found to be associated with phosphorylated tau across a broad age range, while it was only associated with cerebral amyloidosis in the oldest individuals and those with more advanced neurodegeneration 47, 48 .

text.text: Similar relationships between vascular risk factors and their differential effects on AD-tau versus amyloid have been observed with arterial stiffness 49 , hypertension 50 , and Framingham risk score 50 .
text.formatted: Similar relationships between vascular risk factors and their differential effects on AD-tau versus amyloid have been observed with arterial stiffness <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">49</ref> , hypertension <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50</ref> , and Framingham risk score <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">50</ref> .

text.text: The consistent pattern between various vascular risk factors and AD-tau pathophysiology may suggest a common mechanism.
Both blood pressure variability and pulse pressure are associated with decreased cerebral perfusion for example, particularly in vulnerable medial temporal regions [2] [3] [4] 51.
text.formatted: Both blood pressure variability and pulse pressure are associated with decreased cerebral perfusion for example, particularly in vulnerable medial temporal regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">51</ref>.

text.text: The strong relationship between BPV and plasma GFAP observed in the present study may offer additional insight.
Astrocytes are exquisitely sensitive to cerebrovascular pressure changes, acting as intracranial baroreceptors [52] [53] [54] [55] .
text.formatted: Astrocytes are exquisitely sensitive to cerebrovascular pressure changes, acting as intracranial baroreceptors <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[52]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[55]</ref> .

text.text: Sudden changes in cerebral perfusion pressure may trigger astrocyte reactivity 52, 53, [56] [57] [58] [59] [60] , and prior studies show that astrocyte reactivity is a key mechanism component of tau hyperphosphorylation in AD 35, 39, 61, 62 .

text.text: BPV may predispose astrocytes to a reactive phenotype, as its relationship with plasma GFAP suggests, which merits further study.
Limitations include the cross-sectional nature of the study, which limits causal inference.
Strengths include the adjustment for numerous relevant covariates, including the primary genetic risk factor for AD, APOE4 63 , and plasma amyloid-β 42/40 ratio where applicable.

text.text: Future longitudinal studies are needed to confirm the temporal relationships between BPV and AD-tau.

Importantly, the authors recognize that both amyloid-β 42/40 and plasma p-Tau 217 closely track amyloid deposition, however plasma amyloid-β 42/40 generally plateaus relatively early in the AD continuum, while the sharpest upward trajectory and dynamic range of plasma p-Tau 217 tightly parallel the widespread distribution of concurrent amyloid and tau pathophysiology [64] [65] [66] [67] [68] .
text.formatted: Importantly, the authors recognize that both amyloid-β 42/40 and plasma p-Tau 217 closely track amyloid deposition, however plasma amyloid-β 42/40 generally plateaus relatively early in the AD continuum, while the sharpest upward trajectory and dynamic range of plasma p-Tau 217 tightly parallel the widespread distribution of concurrent amyloid and tau pathophysiology <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[64]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[65]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[66]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[67]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[68]</ref> .

text.text: Plasma p-Tau 217 is a measure of tau hyperphosphorylation that occurs in the presence of amyloid-β 65, 69 a unique feature of AD progression, as reflected in the Core 1 T1 classification of p-Tau 217 in the most recent recommendations for the diagnosis and staging of AD 31 .
text.formatted: Plasma p-Tau 217 is a measure of tau hyperphosphorylation that occurs in the presence of amyloid-β <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">65,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">69</ref> a unique feature of AD progression, as reflected in the Core 1 T1 classification of p-Tau 217 in the most recent recommendations for the diagnosis and staging of AD <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">31</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, while both plasma amyloid-β 42/40 and plasma p-Tau 217 track amyloid-β deposition, the biomarkers represent clinically distinct states of AD progression and are therefore well-suited for testing the effects of elevated BPV on AD pathophysiology.
The present study findings are highly consistent with prior research, including the observed relationships with Core 1 T 1 22 , and the relationship with plasma GFAP 10 .
text.formatted: The present study findings are highly consistent with prior research, including the observed relationships with Core 1 T 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22</ref> , and the relationship with plasma GFAP <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> .

text.text: Importantly however, the present study adds the novel and clinically significant finding that elevated beat-tobeat BPV is associated with plasma p-Tau 217 independent of blood pressure level which suggests BPV is a distinct vascular risk factor for AD, and that beat-to-beat BPV screening may be an important non-invasive early biomarker of Alzheimer's disease.
